extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, painters, creative writers, and students of aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for producing and evaluating the sublime and the beautiful in literature and the arts — how certain passions, distance/modification, sympathy, imitation, and social motives generate aesthetic effects. Useful for writers, dramatists, and visual artists aiming to elicit specific emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of the Sublime: pain, danger, and terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is fitted in any sort to excite the ideas of pain and danger; that is to say, whatever is in any sort terrible, or is conversant about terrible objects, or operates in a manner analogous to terror, is a source of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sublime produces the strongest emotion the mind can feel. Ideas of pain and especially death are more powerful than pleasures. When danger or pain press too nearly they are simply terrible; at certain distances or with modifications they may be delightful (see distance/modification entry). Examples and emphasis: the torments of execution, the king of terrors (death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance and modification convert terror into delight
rubrics_metrics.description: When danger or pain are presented at a certain distance, or with certain modifications, they may be delightful rather than simply terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind can find delight in the idea of pain/danger when it is not imminent. This explains why representations of fearful things (tragedy, ruins, catastrophe in history) can give pleasure: the emotion is strong but not actually threatening the spectator. Use controlled distance and modification to evoke sublime delight without real harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pleasure and delight (relative pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are pleasures and pains of a positive and independent nature; the feeling which results from the ceasing or diminution of pain does not resemble positive pleasure and should be distinguished — the author calls the relative pleasure 'delight'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'pleasure' for positive, independent satisfactions and 'delight' for satisfactions that arise from the removal or mitigation of pain/danger. The removal of pain can produce a very real feeling, different in cause and effect from positive pleasure; the author purposely limits 'delight' to this relative sense to avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of cessation of pleasure: indifference, disappointment, grief
rubrics_metrics.description: The cessation of pleasure affects the mind three ways: simple cessation after proper time produces indifference; abrupt breaking produces disappointment; total and irretrievable loss produces grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distinctions inform how readers/audiences experience loss in narrative: indifference, disappointment, and grief are qualitatively different responses and none of them resemble positive pain. Grief often contains pleasurable elements (dwellings on past pleasures), which affects how characters and readers sustain sorrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions of self-preservation vs passions of society
rubrics_metrics.description: Most ideas that make a powerful impression reduce to two heads: self-preservation and society. Passions concerning self-preservation turn mostly on pain and danger and are the most powerful; social passions mainly on pleasures and gratifications (especially generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting strong emotional effects, consider whether the material appeals to self-preservation (fear, horror, sublimity) or social/sexual motives (love, attachment, beauty). Self-preservation passions tend to be stronger; social passions can motivate long-term behavior and attachment. The final causes explain why responses differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as a social quality that inspires love and attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a social quality: when persons or animals give a sense of joy and pleasure in beholding them, they inspire tenderness and affection and fix choice; beauty is the object of the mixed passion called love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish beauty from mere lust (seen in brutes). In human art/characterization, beauty should be used to create social bonds, tenderness, and preference — qualities that make characters or objects desirable companions. This explains how physical or sensible qualities can direct attachment in narrative and visual arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society and solitude: relative pleasures and pains
rubrics_metrics.description: Society merely as society gives no positive pleasure in enjoyment; absolute and perpetual solitude is a great positive pain. Particular social enjoyments, however, give strong pleasurable sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast between companionship (specific social pleasures) and absolute solitude (extreme pain) to heighten stakes. Temporary solitude can be agreeable; total exile or permanent isolation functions as deep suffering. This informs setting and character isolation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy as the mechanism by which art transfuses passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy is a sort of substitution by which we are put into the place of another and affected as he is; it can partake of passions of self-preservation (sublime) or pleasures (social). Poetry, painting, and other arts transfuse their passions by sympathy and can graft delight onto wretchedness, misery, and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To move an audience, create conditions for sympathy: make the spectator mentally substitute into the sufferer's place. Art gains power by prompting automatic, constitution-driven sympathy (not merely reasoned empathy). This explains tragic pleasure and why representations of misfortune can be appealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight in others' distress: mixed pleasure and uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a degree of delight (no small one) in the real misfortunes and pains of others; this delight is blended with uneasiness and prompts relief actions — it both attracts and motivates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic and historical narratives can provoke a compound response: curiosity/delight in calamity plus a moral prompt to relieve. The author argues this is instinctive and not solely the result of reasoning. Use this ambivalence to create complex reader responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of tragedy and the role of imitation versus reality
rubrics_metrics.description: In imitated distresses the pleasure includes the pleasure from imitation. The nearer representation approaches reality, the more powerful its effect; yet the real spectacle would generally outdo the imitative arts (example: a theatre emptied if a real execution occurs nearby).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power of tragic representation depends both on fidelity to reality and on the imitative skill. Recognize a limit: imitation cannot fully equal real events, but improved realism increases aesthetic power. Use heightened verisimilitude and timing to maximize tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation: pleasure in copying and a rule to attribute artistic power
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation (desire to copy) gives pleasure; it is by imitation far more than by precept that we learn and find delight. Rule: if the object represented is one we could have no desire to see in reality, the power of the art is owing to imitation; if we would run to see it in reality, the power is due more to the nature of the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule when deciding whether the effect of a work comes from craft (skill of imitation) or the inherent fascination of the subject. Still-life examples: humble objects give pleasure via imitation; grand events derive power from the subject's nature. This helps writers/artists choose subjects and modes of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition and the inward sense of greatness elicited by the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: God has planted in man a sense of ambition and a satisfaction from excelling others; when without danger we are conversant with terrible objects, the mind claims part of the dignity of those things, producing a sense of inward greatness that fills a reader of sublime passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sublime can make readers feel an elevated inner dignity or triumph. Authors can exploit this by presenting terrible or grand objects in a manner that allows the audience to vicariously 'share' their grandeur without real risk, producing pleasurable ambition/glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapitulation: compact rule for identifying the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions which belong to self-preservation turn on pain and danger; they are simply painful when their causes immediately affect us; they are delightful when we have an idea of pain and danger without being actually in such circumstances; whatever excites this delight is called sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this compact rule as a working definition: to create or evaluate the sublime, present the idea of pain/danger so it strongly affects the imagination while preserving the spectator's safety. This distinction guides composition, tone, and the controlled use of terror in art.
